clue.text: Learn a craft? He's bound to

definitions.text: Learn a craft? He's bound to

parts.words: Learn a craft? He's bound to
parts.note: a trainee who is legally bound by indenture to a master while learning a trade

explanation.surface: Someone asked whether they must learn a trade replies that he is obliged to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' carries the pun: obliged, and also bound by articles of indenture, as a trainee once was.
explanation.definitionFit: A trainee in a trade was formally indentured, bound by contract, to the master teaching the craft.

parts.note: PE is physical education, school exercise
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: Someone checks their training log.
explanation.definitionFit: To peep is to take a quick glance, a synonym for a brief look.

indicators.note: broken signals that the letters of a trio's are smashed and rearranged

explanation.surface: A threesome falls apart and so do its relationships.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges ATRIOS, the letters of 'A trio's'.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratio is a proportional relationship between two quantities.

indicators.note: sounding tells us the word for chivalrous is only heard, not written

parts.note: knightly behaviour is chivalrous, like a knight's

explanation.surface: Someone is always late, yet seems gallant.
explanation.walkthrough: KNIGHTLY, said aloud, loses its silent K.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done every evening happens at a late hour on a regular basis.

clue.text: Outbreak of rain in the country

indicators.note: an outbreak breaks the word rain apart so its letters can be reordered

explanation.surface: A sudden shower of rain falls across the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outbreak of' rearranges the letters of 'rain'.
explanation.definitionFit: Iran is a nation in western Asia, so it is an example of a country.

clue.text: Gemstone-a dealer maybe holds a number

indicators.note: holds means the shuffled letters wrap around the number
maybe suggests the word dealer could be arranged another way

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, a number

explanation.surface: A jeweller is holding a numbered gemstone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges DEALER, and 'holds' puts M inside, giving E-M-ERALD.
explanation.definitionFit: This green precious stone is a variety of beryl.

parts.note: ample means plenty, quite enough
forth means out, as in 'go forth'

explanation.surface: Someone has had quite enough of school and leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: AMPLEFORTH is a well-known Catholic boarding school in North Yorkshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Ampleforth College is a named English independent school, so it is an example.

parts.note: not a pioneer village but a bill settled before it falls due

explanation.surface: A historian describes one of the first villages founded in a region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'settlement' looks like a colony; it is the paying of an account, done in advance.
explanation.definitionFit: Paying in advance means a debt is settled before the usual time.

clue.text: Arab prince recalls Ancient Mariner's story

indicators.note: recalls, read as calls back, signals the poem's title word is read backwards

parts.note: Coleridge's poem is The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

explanation.surface: An Arab ruler retells Coleridge's seafaring tale.
explanation.definitionFit: An emir is a Muslim ruler or commander, a title of Arab nobility.

clue.text: The scale of EEC trading abroad

indicators.note: abroad, meaning astray or scattered widely, signals the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Commentary on how large European Community trade overseas has grown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' rearranges the letters of 'EEC trading'; the EEC was the European Economic Community.
explanation.definitionFit: Celsius temperature measurement divided into a hundred degrees is the scale meant.

clue.text: Arrive to put a map away?

explanation.definitionFit: To turn up is to arrive; a paper map is stored by rolling it into a tube.

clue.text: Messenger has a job getting in beer

indicators.note: getting in means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer
a post is a job or position

explanation.surface: A courier lands a job while fetching the beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has a job' tempts A + POST as a charade, but the A is already the start of the beer that wraps round the job.
explanation.definitionFit: The disciples sent out to spread the gospel were messengers; the Greek root means one sent forth.

clue.text: Staggers, due to ill-fitting satin shoes

indicators.note: ill-fitting suggests the letters of satin shoes are put together wrongly

explanation.surface: Someone totters about because their satin shoes do not fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staggers' looks like a wobbly walk; it means amazes. 'ill-fitting' rearranges 'satin shoes'.
explanation.definitionFit: To stagger someone is to amaze them, a synonym.

parts.note: First World War soldiers climbed out of the trench parapet; the idiom means excessive

explanation.surface: A question about advancing too deep between the trenches.
explanation.walkthrough: In the First World War, attacking troops climbed out of the trenches into no-man's land; the phrase now means going too far.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means excessive, and literally describes leaving the trench to cross no-man's land.

parts.note: a sea duck, and also 'either' spoken in a comic accent where th becomes d

explanation.surface: A comic voice asks which of two ducks is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dis' and 'dat' mimic an accent saying 'this' and 'that'; 'this or that' is 'either', which in the same accent is said with a D.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a large sea duck prized for its down, and the accent turns 'either' into its name.

parts.note: a belt is a hard blow
fly is informal for smart or knowing

explanation.surface: Someone straps a belt on and looks smart in blue.
explanation.definitionFit: A bluebottle is a type of fly that lays eggs on meat, which this kind does.
A knife's cutting edge; and, in old slang, a dashing young man about town.
To surrender is to give up; the dividend return on shares is their income.
Fastening with string secures something; drawn matches end in level scores.

clue.text: The charge is about right, but you don't have to pay

indicators.note: is about means the charge surrounds the letter for right

parts.note: a fee is a charge

explanation.surface: A price has been set fairly, yet there is no need to pay it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is about' puts R inside FEE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something costing nothing is something no payment is needed for.

parts.note: not lawsuits but legal documents, or simply acts done lawfully

explanation.surface: A question about lawsuits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Legal actions' suggests lawsuits; the answer is acts, and also documents such as title papers to a house.
explanation.definitionFit: These are acts, and also formal legal documents such as property title papers.
Arid barren wastelands; and what one deserves, as in 'just deserts'.

parts.note: not an argument for textbooks but the bag a pupil carries them in

explanation.surface: An argument in favour of school textbooks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The case for' reads like an argument; it is a literal bag.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil's shoulder bag holds books, so it is literally a case for them.
Neater, more stylish; and Jean-Marc Nattier, eighteenth-century French portraitist.

clue.text: Listeners burning to get within hearing distance

parts.note: ears are the organs we listen with
hot means burning

explanation.surface: Someone with burning ears is eavesdropping from close by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listeners' is a playful name for ears.
explanation.definitionFit: The range within which one can hear something is the distance meant.
To school is to train; RUGBY is a famous English public school where the game began.

parts.note: the idiom 'laugh up one's ...' means to be secretly amused

explanation.surface: A question of where to giggle privately.
explanation.walkthrough: To laugh up one's sleeve is to be secretly amused.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names the arm of a garment as where hidden mirth goes.

clue.text: He's against the proposal and ain't going to change!

indicators.note: going to change says the letters of ain't will be rearranged

explanation.surface: An opponent of a plan says he won't budge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going to change' rearranges AINT; the clue says the opposite of 'won't change' on the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An opponent of a proposal is someone opposed, which this word means as a noun.

indicators.note: in places the word for work inside the symbol for silver

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
to go means to work, function

explanation.surface: Someone is keen to work with silver.
explanation.definitionFit: Being agog means excited and eager to know.
Running someone through is skewering them; a practice performance is also so called.

indicators.note: setting is a jewel's mount, so the words that follow hold the school's name within them

explanation.surface: A school that sets the tone for others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setting' acts as a mount housing the letters, which run across 'thE TONe'; ETON is an elite English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton College is a famous English public school, so it is an example of one.

clue.text: Club gets convict into hellish trouble

indicators.note: into means the convict is placed inside
trouble means disturbance, so the letters of hellish are stirred up

parts.note: a lag is a convict, as in 'old lag'

explanation.surface: A convict brings a club into a hellish situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' signals the convict going inside the shuffled letters; a SHILLELAGH is an Irish blackthorn cudgel, and LAG is British slang for a convict.
explanation.definitionFit: An Irish wooden cudgel, a heavy stick used as a weapon.
